Title: Characterization of geodesic completeness for landmark space
Abstract: We provide a full characterization of geodesic completeness for spaces of configurations of
landmarks with smooth Riemannian metrics that satisfy a rotational and translation invariance
and which are induced from metrics on subgroups of the diffeomorphism group for the shape
domain.
These spaces are widely used for applications in shape analysis, for example, for
measuring shape changes in medical imaging and morphometrics in biology. For statistics of
such data to be well-defined, it is imperative to know if geodesics exist for all times. We extend
previously known sufficient conditions for geodesic completeness based on the regularity of the
metric to give a full characterization for smooth Riemannian metrics with a rotational and
translation invariance by means of an integrability criterion that involves only the behavior of
the cometric kernel as landmarks approach collision. We further use the integrability criterion
for geodesic completeness and previous work on stochastic completeness to construct a family of
Riemannian landmark manifolds that are geodesically complete but stochastically incomplete.

Introduction
In shape analysis, particularly the large deformation diffeomorphic mapping framework (LDDMM),
see, for example, [12, 13, 14], subgroups of the diffeomorphism group of a shape domain are equipped
with right-invariant metrics, typically arising from Sobolev operators. Diffeomorphisms act on a
large number of shape spaces, and, due to the right-invariance, such metrics descend to orbit
shape spaces. One of the most fundamental of such cases is when shapes are configurations of
finite sets of ordered distinct landmarks in Rd, denoted by x = (x1, . . . , xn) where xi ∈Rd and
xi ̸= xj for i, j ∈{1, . . . , n} with i ̸= j. The action of a suitable diffeomorphism ϕ ∈Diff(Rd)
is then by composition from the left, that is, ϕ.x = (ϕ(x1), . . . , ϕ(xn)), and the induced metric
gives the landmark configuration space the structure of a finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold,
as introduced in [7]. These spaces have been the subject of intensive interest in the literature,
both mathematically as in [9, 10] and for applications in, among others, medical imaging and

represent points of interest on datasets of shapes, extending shape statistics as seen in Kendall’s
shape space beyond the Euclidean setting. Such statistics are often based on geodesics between
point configurations. Therefore, both for theoretical interest and for applications, it is important
to know if Riemannian landmark manifolds are geodesically complete.
For n ≥2 and d ≥1 fixed, let (M, g) denote the landmark configuration space consisting of n
distinct landmarks in Rd. In particular, the manifold M is given by
M = {x = (x1, . . . , xn) : x1, . . . , xn ∈Rd with xi ̸= xj for i ̸= j} ⊂Rnd.
When the Riemannian metric g is inherited from a right-invariant weak Riemannian metric on
a suitable subgroup of the diffeomorphism group Diff(Rd), it can be described uniquely by its
cometric that takes the form
gij(x) = K(xi, xj),
for i, j ∈{1, . . . , n} and a positive-definite symmetric kernel K : Rd × Rd →Rd×d. Throughout the
article, we assume that the cometric kernel K is rotationally and translationally invariant so that
there exists a continuous scalar function K: [0, ∞) →R such that
K(xi, xj) = K(∥xi −xj∥)Id,
where ∥· ∥is the Euclidean norm on Rd and Id is the d × d identity matrix. In particular, we then
have, for all i, j ∈{1, . . . , n},
gij(x) = K(∥xi −xj∥)Id.
(1)
As a consequence of Schoenberg [11, Theorem 3], the function K: [0, ∞) →R is guaranteed to be
positive and strictly decreasing.
Geodesics on the Riemannian manifold (M, g) can be studied by lifting to a suitable subgroup
of Diff(Rd). As discussed by Bauer, Bruveris and Michor in [1], since geodesics of diffeomorphisms
are well-defined for all times if K ∈C1(Rd × Rd, Rd×d) and because geodesics on the landmark
space arise as projections of certain geodesics of diffeomorphisms, we have the following sufficient
condition for geodesic completeness.
Theorem 1 (Bauer–Bruveris–Michor [1]). Let (M, g) be the landmark space for any number of
landmarks in any Rd. If K ∈C1(Rd ×Rd, Rd×d) then (M, g) is geodesically complete. Furthermore,
if K ∈C2(Rd × Rd, Rd×d) then (M, g) is metrically complete.
The second part of Theorem 1 follows from an application of the Hopf–Rinow theorem, which in
the C2 case gives the equivalence between geodesic completeness and metric completeness. While
the above approach covers a large class of metrics, geodesic completeness results for (M, g) with
metrics corresponding to non-C1 cometric kernels have so far not been established.
In this article, we fully characterize geodesic completeness for landmark spaces subject to the
assumed rotational and translational invariance in terms of a single integrability criterion for the
scalar function K: [0, ∞) →R close to zero, that is, close to landmarks colliding. Specifically, we
prove the following theorem that does not assume K ∈C1(Rd × Rd, Rd×d).

1.1
Paper outline
In Section 2, we revisit the Hamiltonian formulation of the geodesic equation on landmark spaces
and we prove conservation of the total linear momentum as well as of the total angular momentum.
We use this in Section 3 to prove Proposition 3, that is, the part of Theorem 2 which guarantees
geodesic incompleteness. We proceed by proving Proposition 4, that is, the part of Theorem 2
which ensures geodesic completeness, in Section 4. We continue by demonstrating in Section 5
that Theorem 5 indeed provides examples of landmark spaces that are geodesically complete but
stochastically incomplete. We then close by analyzing the two-landmark system in more detail in
Section 6 and, in particular, by establishing Theorem 6 that the presence of non-zero total angular
momentum in this case prevents finite-time breakdown.

Hamiltonian dynamics on landmark space
For the landmark manifold (M, g), the easiest way to derive the geodesic equation is to take the
Hamiltonian approach on the cotangent bundle T ⋆M. This is due to the Hamiltonian approach

more than two landmarks.

2.1
Combinatorial and geometric methods
The key idea is to use the Hamiltonian formulation to exploit the fact that the cometric K is
invariant under the action of the rotation group SO(d) and the translation group Td. This
invariance reduces the complexity of the problem by allowing us to reduce the dynamics to the
orbit space under the group action, i.e., to the space of relative configurations. The reduced
dynamics can then be analyzed in terms of the relative positions of the landmarks, leading to a
simplification of the problem that is amenable to both combinatorial and geometric methods.

2.2
Combinatorial methods
The combinatorial approach is based on the fact that the landmarks are indistinct, so we can
consider the unordered configuration of landmarks. This leads to the notion of the configuration
space being a manifold with corners, where the corners correspond to the collision set C.
The combinatorial method allows us to count the number of ways the landmarks can collide,
and to analyze the behavior of geodesics near these collisions. This is crucial for establishing the
integrability condition for the geodesic completeness.

2.3
Geometric methods
The geometric approach is based on the analysis of the geodesic equations in the cotangent bundle
T ⋆M. By using the Hamiltonian formulation, we can derive the equations of motion and analyze
their behavior near the collision set C. This involves studying the behavior of the momenta p(t) and
positions x(t) as t approaches the collision time, and showing whether the geodesics can be extended
beyond that time or not.

2.4
Complementary perspectives
The combination of combinatorial and geometric methods provides a comprehensive understanding
of the problem. The combinatorial perspective allows us to count the number of possible collisions,
while the geometric perspective provides the tools to analyze the behavior of the geodesics near
the collision set. Together, these perspectives give a complete picture of the geodesic completeness
of the landmark space.

Proof of Theorem 2
We now outline the proof of Theorem 2, which establishes the equivalence between geodesic
completeness and the integrability condition (2).

First, we consider the case where the cometric kernel K is smooth on (0, ∞). We then analyze
the behavior of the geodesic paths near the collision set C. We show that if the integral (2) converges,
then the geodesics cannot be extended beyond a certain finite time, leading to geodesic incompleteness.
Conversely, if the integral (2) diverges, we show that every geodesic can be extended to all times,
leading to geodesic completeness.

2.6
Proof of Proposition 3
To prove Proposition 3, we consider a specific geodesic path that leads to a finite-time collision.
We construct an initial condition such that the landmarks collide in finite time, and show that this
leads to geodesic incompleteness.
